title: Chemical equations — conserving every atom
summary: Count atoms on each side and change coefficients until matter is conserved.

sections.title: 1. Atoms are rearranged, not lost
sections.markdown: A chemical equation must have the same number of each kind of atom before and after the reaction. In $2H_2 + O_2 → 2H_2O$, both sides contain 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms.

visualization.title: Atoms before and after a reaction
visualization.aria_label: Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule rearrange into two water molecules while atom counts stay equal.
visualization.text_fallback: Reactants have four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms. Products have the same counts in two water molecules.

sections.title: 2. Change coefficients, never subscripts
sections.markdown: A **coefficient** changes how many molecules participate. A **subscript** changes the substance itself. Balance $N_2 + H_2 → NH_3$ as $N_2 + 3H_2 → 2NH_3$.

sections.title: 3. Use an atom-count table
sections.markdown: List every element and count it on the left and right. Adjust one coefficient at a time, recount, and reduce the final coefficients to the smallest whole-number ratio.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.instructions: Enter the requested coefficient or atom count as a whole number.

questions.prompt: In $2H_2 + O_2 → 2H_2O$, what is the coefficient of water?
questions.feedback: Read the number immediately before H₂O.

questions.prompt: In the same equation, what is the coefficient of oxygen?
In $N_2 + 3H_2 → 2NH_3$, what is the coefficient of hydrogen?
In that equation, what is the coefficient of ammonia?
How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of $C_3H_8$?
questions.feedback: The carbon subscript gives the count.
